column1: # Some applications keep genuine user data inside directories whose names say
# "cache". A path-based scanner cannot know that, so it is recorded here.
# The canonical example is Spotify: offline downloads live under its cache
# directory, and cleaners have proposed deleting users' entire music libraries
#   risk  review | risky  -- never "safe"; these rows exist to downgrade trust

column3: Spotify stores offline downloads inside its cache directory. Removing this deletes music you saved for offline listening, which must then be re-downloaded.
iCloud Drive's local file provider state. Removing it can force a full re-sync and evict local copies.
iCloud Documents state; removing it can trigger a full re-download.
Adobe keeps media cache and previews here; removing them forces lengthy re-rendering of video previews.
Photos-managed caches; manage these through Photos rather than by deletion.
Steam keeps shader caches and partial downloads alongside game data.
Docker Desktop's VM disk image lives here. Use docker's own prune commands instead.
OrbStack VM data. Use OrbStack or docker prune commands rather than deleting files.
OneDrive local state; removing it can force a full re-sync.

column1: # Sync clients and virtual machines. These are the Spotify case for people who
# use different software: a directory named "cache" that actually holds either
# the only local copy of a file or a live VM disk. Every row here is a fact
# about that application, and a row for software you do not have simply never

column3: Dropbox's local state and cache. Removing it forces a full re-sync and can evict local copies of files that are only stored online.
Google Drive's local state. Removing it forces a full re-sync and can evict locally available files.
Google Drive File Stream content cache. This holds the local copies of files marked available offline.
Parallels virtual machine data. These are live VM disks, not a cache.
UTM virtual machine data. These are live VM disks, not a cache.
VMware Fusion virtual machine data. These are live VM disks, not a cache.
Adobe Creative Cloud keeps synced libraries and assets here, not only cache.
Backblaze keeps backup state here; removing it can force a full re-scan of the backup set.
